messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The afternoon Kwame was deployed to the valley had been thick with dry dust and the sharp scent of diesel exhaust from the Humvees. When the detonation cracked overhead, it was sudden and loud, tearing through the hum of the patrol. He remembered the precise angle of the blast, the way the dust plumed in a sudden, bruised cloud, and the high whine of Chinooks cutting through the smoke. What stayed with him most was the olfactory echo: even now, when he thinks of that day, the sharp tang of burnt fuel and heated earth rises unbidden, mirroring the smells that had been present during the frightening event. His memories of the engagement do not fade like ordinary recollections; they arrive with a clarity that makes them feel more real and vivid than ordinary memories. He can trace every detail—the rustle of gear, the clipped radio calls, the sudden stillness before the orders came. The event sits in his mind not as a past story, but as something that merely paused. In the months after returning to the American Midwest, Kwame found his attention fixed outward. He was certain that unexpected or loud sounds carried a quiet threat, so his posture tightened the moment a car backfired or a door slammed. He watched the people around him closely, reading their faces and movements for any flicker of harm or surprise. While patrolling the trails at his job as a park ranger, his eyes constantly swept the tree line, the parking lots, and the visitor pathways, cataloguing anything that might shift. When an air tour helicopter approached the valley, the familiar rotor beat would meet him in the open. His chest tightened with discomfort, and a quiet, detached unreality settled over him, as if the world had grown slightly out of reach. He had come to believe he must remain on guard all the time, that letting his shoulders drop even for a moment would leave him exposed. As the weeks turned to months, Kwame’s cautious routines solidified into habits. He avoided the ridge trails during peak flight hours. The sound consistently met his attention, and his hands would linger on his equipment, double-checking straps and zippers. The inaction guilt he carried from the combat zone coexisted with his daily observations; he kept returning to the memory of those final, breathless seconds, certain he would never forgive himself for not moving faster, for not doing more to stop what happened. He felt permanently changed for the worse, as if a piece of his former ease had been lost to the dust. With his wife, Amara, he learned to watch her carefully, noting how her quiet sighs or sudden movements might signal strain. His constant alertness ran alongside his marriage, and his crew has noticed how he hesitates to delegate tasks, the occupational consequence of his vigilance becoming clear in the quiet gaps between assignments. Now, at forty-six, Kwame stands in the ranger station with the morning light filtering through the pines, his radio crackling with visitor reports. The sound of a maintenance truck reversing pulls his head up, and he feels the old discomfort ripple through him, followed quickly by that familiar sense of detachment. He knows he can no longer sustain the endless watching. His PCL-5 score of thirty-three sits quietly beside his daily reality. What he hopes for is simply to hear the sky without bracing, to let the past stay where it belongs, and to believe, even for an hour, that he is safe exactly as he is. He seeks help as the stillness begins to feel heavier than the alertness, and he fears that if he does not learn to rest without looking away, he will lose what remains of his life in the valley.
